extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining prior art, exceptions, effective filing dates, and obviousness rejections under pre-AIA and AIA versions of 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, including use of MPEP form paragraphs and examiner practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.21.fti use for pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) references
rubrics_metrics.description: This paragraph is used to reject over a reference (patent or published application) with an earlier filing date that discloses the claimed invention, and that only qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use this form paragraph if the reference qualifies as prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b) (use form paragraph 7.21.fti only for 102(e)-only situations; use form paragraph 7.21.fti alternatives otherwise). The reference must have either a common assignee, a common applicant (35 U.S.C. 118), or at least one common joint inventor. Do not use when the reference is disqualified under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as prior art in a pre-AIA 103(a) rejection. Include the appropriate claim numbers and prior art reference identifiers in the brackets per Examiner Notes and see MPEP § 2146 et seq. for assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIPA/AIPA application of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as amended by the American Inventors Protection Act of 1999 (AIPA) must be applied if the reference is by another and is one of the following: (a) a U.S. patent or a publication of a U.S. application for patent filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a); (b) a U.S. patent issued directly or indirectly from, or a U.S. or WIPO publication of, an international application (PCT) if the international application has an international filing date on or after November 29, 2000; (c) a U.S. patent issued from, or a WIPO publication of, an international design application that designates the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Examiner Notes for form paragraph 7.12.fti or 7.12.01.fti to assist in determination of the applicable pre-AIA 102(e) date; apply pre-AIPA rules only to U.S. patents issued from international applications filed prior to November 29, 2000 as described in the MPEP notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.22.fti (Further in View Of) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over [2] as applied to claim [3] above, and further in view of [4].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.21.fti. An explanation of the rejection must follow this form paragraph (see MPEP § 2144). If the rejection relies on prior art under pre-AIA 102(e), determine the reference’s 102(e) date using the AIPA rules unless the reference is a U.S. patent issued from an international application with an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000 (see MPEP § 2146 guidance and Examiner Notes for 7.12.fti and 7.12.01.fti).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for Obviousness (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows: 1) Determining the scope and contents of the prior art. 2) Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue. 3) Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. 4) Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this four-factor test to frame obviousness analyses and as a response to arguments about applicability of the factors. Provide factual findings that map to these inquiries when making or explaining an obviousness rejection (see MPEP § 2144).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.27.fti for alternative 102/103 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim(s) [1] is/are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102([2]) as anticipated by or, in the alternative, under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over [3].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended to substitute for making a single appropriate rejection under 102 or 103 when practicable. Appropriate uses include: (a) disputed claim interpretation where one interpretation supports 102 and another supports 103; (b) where reference discloses all limitations except a property or function and examiner cannot determine inherent properties; (c) genus/species issues; (d) product-by-process equivalence issues; (e) means-plus-function equivalence or obvious variant uncertainty; (f) overlapping ranges without explicit example. If claim interpretation renders claim indefinite, consider 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection. Bracket instructions: insert claim numbers, paragraph letters, and references per Examiner Notes. A full explanation must follow. Precede this paragraph with the listed form paragraphs (7.07.fti, relevant 7.08–7.14.fti, 7.20.fti or 7.103) and for certain filings include 7.06 where applicable (see MPEP for details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued applicability of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA revisions to 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 do not apply to any application filed before March 16, 2013; such applications are governed by pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (pre-AIA applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an RCE or entry into the national stage under 35 U.S.C. 371 does not create a new application or change this status. Submission of amendments adding new matter after March 16, 2013 does not change pre-AIA status. PCT applications filed under 35 U.S.C. 363 before March 16, 2013 remain pre-AIA regardless of national stage timing. Applications filed on/after March 16, 2013 may nonetheless be subject to pre-AIA 102 if they never contained a claim with effective filing date on/after March 16, 2013 or never claimed benefit of an application that contained such a claim (see MPEP §§ 2131–2138).

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) definitions of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) provides that a person is not entitled to a patent if the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention. AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) provides that a person is not entitled to a patent if the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under 35 U.S.C. 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b), in which the patent or application names another inventor, and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must note the unchanged introductory phrase '[a] person shall be entitled to a patent unless', preserving the Office's initial burden to explain rejections. The categories of prior art documents and activities are set forth in 102(a)(1) (documents and public activities) and 102(a)(2) (U.S. patent documents). Use appropriate documentary evidence (issued patents, published applications, non-patent literature) or evidence of public use/sale to support rejections; printed publications can sometimes be used as evidence of prior public use or sale when their own date is not sufficiently early (see In re Epstein and MPEP § 2133.03(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) one-year grace period exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure made 1 year or less before the effective filing date of a claimed invention shall not be prior art under 102(a)(1) if (A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or a joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor; or (B) the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a one-year grace period measured from the filing date of the earliest U.S. or foreign patent application to which a proper benefit/priority is asserted and that supports the claimed invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Under pre-AIA 102(b) the one-year grace period was measured from the earliest U.S. filing date; under AIA it is measured from the earliest application to which benefit is properly claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of WIPO/PCT publications and U.S. patent documents under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A WIPO publication of a PCT international application that designates the United States is an application for patent deemed published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b) for purposes of AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2). Thus, WIPO published PCT applications that designate the U.S., U.S. patents, or U.S. patent application publications that name another inventor and were effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention are prior art under AIA 102(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO publications of PCT applications are treated as U.S. patent application publications for prior art purposes regardless of international filing date, language, or whether the PCT entered the U.S. national stage. Under pre-AIA 102(e) different rules applied (e.g., PCT filing date thresholds and language/publishing considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) definition of 'effectively filed' for U.S. patent documents
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. patent document is considered to have been effectively filed for prior art effect under 102(a)(2) as of the earlier of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or the application for patent; or (2) if the patent or application is entitled to claim the benefit of, or priority to, an earlier U.S. provisional, nonprovisional, international (PCT), or foreign patent application, the filing date of the earliest such application that describes the subject matter of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the prior art effect of U.S. patent documents from the effective filing date (earliest application to which benefit/priority is claimed that describes the relied-upon subject matter), regardless of whether that earliest application is a U.S. provisional/nonprovisional, international (PCT), or foreign application. Use AIA 102(d) to determine whether a U.S. patent document predates a claimed invention's effective filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2) exceptions to prior art in 102(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure shall not be prior art to a claimed invention under 102(a)(2) if (A) the subject matter disclosed was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor; (B) the subject matter disclosed had, before such subject matter was effectively filed under 102(a)(2), been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor; or (C) the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions can remove certain U.S. patent documents from being prior art under 102(a)(2), including co-worker/collaborator disclosures, but do not remove disclosures that are prior art under 102(a)(1) (patents, printed publications, public uses, sales, or other public disclosures) unless they also meet the 102(b)(1) exceptions. Consider both the source of the disclosure and ownership/assignment status when applying these exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership/joint research agreement exception (AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 100(h) 'joint research agreement' is a written contract/grant/cooperative agreement between two or more persons or entities for experimental/developmental/research work in the field of the claimed invention. 35 U.S.C. 102(c) provides that subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to assignment to the same person in applying 102(b)(2)(C) if: (1) the subject matter disclosed was developed and the claimed invention was made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; (2) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (3) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three-part test to determine whether the common ownership exception applies. The exception operates to treat disclosures made pursuant to the joint research agreement as commonly owned for the purposes of 102(b)(2)(C), potentially removing certain disclosures as prior art under 102(a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination or replacement of certain pre-AIA 102 provisions under the AIA
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA eliminates the provisions in pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) (abandonment), 102(d) (foreign patenting), 102(f) (derivation handled elsewhere), and 102(g) (prior invention by another) as they previously existed; some provisions are replaced or their effects limited (see discussion of continued limited applicability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the AIA, abandonment or premature foreign patenting are not relevant to patentability. Situations formerly handled under pre-AIA 102(f) are now addressed in derivation proceedings (35 U.S.C. 135), correction of inventorship (37 CFR 1.48), or rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115. Be aware of limited continued applicability (e.g., pre-AIA 102(g) may still apply to certain claims in AIA applications as described in MPEP § 2151).

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness standard and temporal focus
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 provides that a patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art. The temporal focus for the obviousness inquiry is before the effective filing date of the claimed invention rather than at the time of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tracks pre-AIA 103(a) substantively but shifts the temporal benchmark to effective filing date. The provisions of pre-AIA 103(c) have been replaced with AIA 102(b)(2)(C) and (c); biochemical/process-specific 103(b) provisions have been eliminated. Ensure obviousness analyses use the effective filing date as the temporal reference and account for any changed exceptions under the AIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office burden and requirements when making rejections (35 U.S.C. 132 and related MPEP guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA preserves the requirement that whenever a claim for a patent is rejected or an objection or requirement is made, the Office shall notify the applicant and state the reasons for such rejection, objection, or requirement, and provide such information and references as may be useful to the applicant in judging the propriety of continuing the prosecution of the application (see 35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.104(c) and MPEP § 706).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must identify and explain the statutory/regulatory basis of rejections, include references and factual findings supporting the rejection, and provide sufficient information for the applicant to respond meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective filing date of the claimed invention (AIA 35 U.S.C. 100(i) and MPEP § 2152.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA defines 'effective filing date' for a claimed invention as the earlier of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or application containing the claimed invention; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application for which the patent or application is entitled to a right of priority or the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 121, 365, or 386 (see 35 U.S.C. 100(i)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In examining AIA 102 issues, the effective filing date is generally the actual U.S. filing date unless specific situations apply (continuation/divisional/national stage/priority/benefit per 35 U.S.C. 120, 365(c), 386(c), etc.). The MPEP lists situations (A)-(D) that can cause the effective filing date to be earlier; e.g., (A) if the application is a continuation or divisional and requirements of 35 U.S.C. 120, 365(c), or 386(c) are satisfied, the effective filing date is the earliest filing date in the line. Follow MPEP § 2152.01 for detailed determination steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA prevents antedating/'swearing behind' certain prior art disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the AIA the date of invention is not relevant for determining prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102; it is no longer possible to antedate or 'swear behind' certain prior art disclosures by showing that the applicant invented the claimed invention prior to the effective date of the prior art disclosure (e.g., via 37 CFR 1.131).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on invention date evidence to overcome disclosures that are prior art under AIA 102(a); focus analyses on effective filing dates, documented prior disclosures, and applicable exceptions (102(b)). Where applicable, consider derivation proceedings or correction of inventorship for disputes about who was the actual inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories and evidentiary sources for prior art under AIA 102(a)(1) and 102(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents upon which a prior art rejection under 102(a)(1) may be based include an issued patent, a published application, a non-patent printed publication, and evidence that the claimed invention was in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public. Documents for a 102(a)(2) rejection are U.S. patent documents only (including WIPO PCT publications deemed published under 122(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that printed publications that lack an early enough publication date may nonetheless serve as competent evidence of earlier public use or sale activity. Use relevant case law (e.g., In re Epstein) and MPEP § 2133.03(b) when relying on documentary evidence to establish public availability or dates.
